Lessons.Title: Another Addition Algorithm
ExplanationParagraphs: Another Addition Algorithm: build on partial-sums recording to develop a written method that places one digit in each place-value position. Newly composed tens or hundreds must be recorded rather than discarded. This is grounded in place-value understanding, not a memorized symbol rule.

Warm-up — Notice and Wonder: Another Curious Table (10 minutes). Row and column headers are 98, 99, 100, 101 and 102. In the row for 100, the two question-mark cells under columns 99 and 101 are 199 and 201. Notice symmetry of 98+99=99+98=197, odd/even sum patterns, and sums staying equal from bottom-left to top-right; the teacher reviews observations instead of requiring all missing table cells.

Activity 1 — A New Addition Algorithm (15 minutes). Compare Han and Elena for 367+231=598. Han writes the partial sums 8 (ones), 90 (tens), and 500 (hundreds), then combines 8+90+500. Elena records a single digit for each place position, building 8 ones, 9 tens and 5 hundreds as 598. Explain why both algorithms add the same like units and give the same value. The original publisher picture layouts are not embedded; this first-party rendering preserves the mathematics only.

Activity 2 — Compose New Units (20 minutes). On 365+182=547, the ones are 5+2=7, the tens are 60+80=140 (14 tens), and the hundreds are 300+100=400. Han may record 7+140+400. Elena writes 7 ones and 4 tens with a composed hundred, giving 5 hundreds, 4 tens, 7 ones. Both methods account for the full 14 tens. Partner discussion explains where the new hundred goes.

Students practise Elena's algorithm with 174+352=526, 273+619=892, 354+198=552 and 525+376=901. For 354+198, 4+8=12 ones makes 1 new ten; 50+90+10=150 makes 1 new hundred; 300+100+100=500. The digits are 5 hundreds, 5 tens and 2 ones: 552. For 525+376, compose both a new ten and a hundred to obtain 901, not 801.

Teacher synthesis asks how recording the ten or hundred above the addends and recording partial sums below are connected to place-value exchanges. Pupils explain how the methods differ visually and why they remain equivalent; use MLR8 discussion support and speech or blocks to explain, rather than demanding a solitary scalar response.

The original first-edition teacher lesson suggests independent thinking, partner comparison and teacher-guided conversation; these are recorded as teacher-led elements. Optional centers remain separate and their original sheets have not been copied.

The independently authored Edulytics practice and Cool-down assess addition with composing. They are not the publisher's gated Use an Algorithm for Addition Cool-down. Original source student PDF, algorithm artwork and optional gameboard fidelity remain unverified; no 100% source-material claim is made.

KeyConcepts.Title: Partial sums
KeyConcepts.Definition: One may record all like-unit totals separately.
KeyConcepts.Rule: Add the values for ones, tens, hundreds, then combine them.

KeyConcepts.Title: Single digit per place
KeyConcepts.Definition: The value of a place in the sum is recorded as one digit, with composed units transferred.
KeyConcepts.Rule: 10 ones become one ten; 10 tens become one hundred.
KeyConcepts.Example: 14 tens becomes 4 tens and one hundred.

KeyConcepts.Title: Conservation of value
KeyConcepts.Definition: Different correct records represent the same total.
KeyConcepts.Rule: No carried ten or hundred can disappear.

WorkedExamples.Title: Han and Elena agree
WorkedExamples.Question: Calculate 367+231 in both representations.
WorkedExamples.Method: Separate into like units then record compact digits.

WorkedExamples.Title: Compose 14 tens
WorkedExamples.Question: Add 365 and 182.
WorkedExamples.Method: Record the whole 140 tens-value and exchange for 1 hundred plus 4 tens.

WorkedExamples.Title: Compose tens and hundreds
WorkedExamples.Question: Calculate 354+198.
Steps: 5 tens + 9 tens + 1 carried ten =15 tens: write 5, carry one hundred.

CommonMistakes.WhyWrong: Fourteen tens includes one additional hundred.
CommonMistakes.Correction: Record 140 or one carried hundred plus four tens.

CommonMistakes.Mistake: Treating Elena's step as a different arithmetic rule from Han's.
CommonMistakes.WhyWrong: Both still combine ones with ones, tens with tens, hundreds with hundreds.
CommonMistakes.Correction: Explain the location, not the existence, of the partial sums.

CommonMistakes.WhyWrong: The units and tens both compose new higher units.
CommonMistakes.Correction: 12 ones -> 2 ones plus 1 ten; 15 tens -> 5 tens plus 1 hundred.

CommonMistakes.WhyWrong: A composed hundred has been lost.

CommonMistakes.Mistake: Certifying an algorithm explanation solely from a correct number.
CommonMistakes.WhyWrong: The source requires discussion of the two recordings and place-value transfers.
CommonMistakes.Correction: Teacher judges step sequencing and equivalence explanations.

SummaryPoints: Two central missing entries in the curious table are 199 and 201.
On 365+182, fourteen tens must be represented faithfully; sum=547.
The four source additions are 526,892,552 and 901.
The student compares the algorithms rather than only writing totals.
No original publisher algorithm screenshots or gated Cool-down are asserted as copied.
